newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Minister says Yugo telecom sale to help industry.
newsitem.headline: Minister says Yugo telecom sale to help industry.

text.p: Privatisation Minister Milan Beko said Serbia has yet to make a final decision on how to spend nearly $1 billion from the sale of 49 percent stake in Telekom Srbija, but at least part of it will be used to revamp some state industries.
Nearly one billion dollars is the size of the M1 money supply on which Yugoslavia's economy relies in its day-to-day activity.
"The money is here, but we have not yet decided precisely how to allocate those funds," Beko told Reuters.

According to the agreement sealed earlier this week between Telekom Srbija and Italian and Greek telecom companies Stet and OTE 80 percent of the entire sum was agreed to be paid immediately to Serbian accounts and the rest in January 1998.

"The entire amount (1.254 billion German marks) is in the Serbian banking system. The payment was scheduled within 48 hours from the moment of signing and the money was on our accounts on the 26th hour," the minister added.
The sole recipient of Telekom's money is the Serbian Development Fund and Beko insisted it was unwise to keep the entire amount with one bank only.
Serbian economy, devastated after almost four years of war-related sanctions, is estimated to need around one billion dollars a year to move on.
Economists said around $200 million would be just about enough to give impetus to idling industries, still performing badly at close to 40 percent capacity and with more than 800,000 surplus labour.
"Right now we are absolutely ready to swallow $200 million or $300 million to kick-start the economy," Beko said.

"The money will definitely be used to finance upgrading of big infrastructure systems, support export-oriented programmes and increase production. Every company can select its programmes and apply for some funds," Beko said.

After drafting a list of companies and projects qualifying for the financial support from the Serbian Development Fund, the rest of the money will be put at the disposal of Serbian banks to help them improve their image and credit rating.
"Serbian banks will use the remaining amount for placements strictly according to international financial standards in order to make profit," Beko said.
Putting the Telekom money into Serbian ailing banks was just what most economists feared.

The Institute of Economic Sciences (IEN) cautioned last week that any allocation of funds raised from the Telekom sale must not be conducted through the indebted banking sector before it restructures and consolidates. IEN insisted banks first needed to wave good-bye to big state loss-making firms. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
